title: An ignition figure asks one thing: when does the chemistry outrun the cooling, and does the kernel then sustain itself?
summary: A warm patch either cools back or runs away. The tell-tale is a sharp knee in the hottest-point curve while the domain average barely moves. Reading it means finding the knee, checking what the snapshots show on either side of it, and asking how much of the fuel the burning region has actually consumed.

media.alt: Four temperature snapshots of a 20 mm square domain at 0, 4.8, 6.6 and 24 ms: a diffuse purple warm patch, a slightly hotter patch, a tiny bright spot at the ignition point and a large bright disc of about 11 mm diameter. Below, the hottest-point temperature rises slowly from about 1250 K, then jumps to about 2800 K at 6.6 ms, while the average temperature rises only from about 680 K to 1080 K. A third panel shows fuel consumed rising to about 25 percent at 24 ms.

read_the_figure.question: Does a locally pre-heated patch ignite, and when?
read_the_figure.axes: Top row: four temperature snapshots of a 20 mm by 20 mm domain (x and y in millimetres, shared colour bar from about 300 to 3000 K). Bottom left: temperature in kelvin against time in milliseconds for the hottest point and for the domain average. Bottom right: fuel consumed, as a percentage of the local fuel, against time. The dashed vertical line marks the ignition time in both time plots.
look_at: Find the knee in the red hottest-point curve. Before it, the temperature creeps up from about 1250 K to about 1500 K over almost 5 ms. At the knee it climbs by well over a thousand kelvin in under a millisecond. That is thermal runaway.
Compare with the blue average temperature. It barely moves at the knee, because only a tiny region has ignited. A mean that does not react tells you the event is local.

Match the dashed line to the snapshots. The third snapshot (6.6 ms) shows a very small, very bright spot: the moment of ignition. The fourth shows a bright disc about 11 mm across (from about 4.5 to 15.5 mm): the burning region that has grown from that spot.

After the knee, the red curve is nearly flat, near 2900 K and then slowly falling to about 2750 K. A burning kernel reaching a plateau is a sign the burned state is close to its equilibrium temperature.

The fuel panel is the check that this is combustion rather than heating: it rises steadily after ignition, to about 25 percent at 24 ms. The kernel has become hot much faster than it has consumed fuel.
read_the_figure.proves: The figure shows a single run in which a pre-heated patch passes through a runaway. With a defined ignition marker, it shows what runaway looks like in the four standard views: snapshots, maximum, mean and consumption. It does not show how sensitive ignition is to the size or temperature of the patch; that needs several runs.
if_wrong: No knee and a smoothly rising maximum: the patch is below the ignition threshold, or diffusion removes heat faster than reaction adds it.
A knee in the maximum but no rise in fuel consumed: temperature is being set by something other than reaction (for example an imposed source).
A plateau above the physical flame temperature for the mixture: an energy-balance or property error.
A kernel with grid-sized edges (the fourth snapshot is blocky at its rim): the front is resolved by only a few cells, so its speed and thickness are mesh-dependent.
must_check: Domain size, colour range and units on every panel.
A definition of the ignition time (here the dashed line) and what criterion produced it.
Mixture composition, initial pressure, and patch size and temperature, none of which are printed in the figure.
Mean and maximum both shown, so locality is visible.
Resolution of the kernel front, stated or visible.
as_drawn: Values are read off the plots by eye (about 5 to 10 percent).

Hottest point: about 1250 K at 0 ms, about 1500 K at 4.8 ms, about 1900 K at 6 ms, and about 2800 K at 6.6 ms (the dashed line). The maximum is about 2900 K at 7 to 15 ms, then falls to about 2750 K by 24 ms.
Average temperature: about 680 K at the start, almost flat to 6.6 ms, about 1080 K at 24 ms.
Heating rate of the hottest point: roughly 50 K/ms between 0 and 4.8 ms, and roughly 1500 K/ms between 6.0 and 6.6 ms, a factor of about 30.
Fuel consumed: about 1 percent at the ignition time, about 25 percent at 24 ms.

terms.meaning: The transition from slow warming to a self-accelerating reaction that releases heat faster than it can be removed.
Positive feedback: reaction raises temperature, which raises the reaction rate, which raises temperature further.
The reaction rate constant grows exponentially with temperature, with an activation energy setting how steeply.
A small region hotter than its surroundings, such as a spark or hot particle, used as the trigger for ignition.
The small burning region created by successful ignition, which then grows outward as a flame front.
The time from the start to the runaway. Here it is the time of the dashed line, about 6.6 ms.
Heat diffusing out of the patch into the colder gas. If it exceeds heat release, the patch cools.
Fraction of the initial local fuel that has reacted. It confirms that temperature rise is due to combustion.

remember: Ignition is a competition: heat release against heat loss. The faster-growing one wins.
The reaction rate depends exponentially on temperature, so a small temperature rise can produce a large rate increase.
The maximum shows the event; the mean hides it. Always read both.
A plateau after ignition is the burned-gas temperature, set by energy conservation.
A single run shows one outcome. Whether a patch ignites is a statement about a threshold, which needs several runs.

understand.title: Reading the knee
understand.text: Before ignition the temperature follows a slowly accelerating curve because heat release is small and conduction is removing some of it. Ignition is the moment heat release overtakes loss; then the curve turns almost vertical until the fuel locally gets used up and the temperature saturates.

understand.title: Why the average hardly moves
understand.text: The burning region is small compared with the 20 mm domain at the time of the knee. The mean is dominated by the cold gas, so it carries almost no sign of the event. Only as the disc grows does the mean rise.

understand.title: Why the fuel panel is slower than the temperature panel
understand.text: Temperature responds to the rate of reaction in the hottest few cells. The consumed fraction counts fuel over the region considered, so it integrates over a larger volume and over time. Temperature has a knee, consumption a steady slope.

steps.title: The rate depends exponentially on temperature
steps.note: Standard Arrhenius form. The activation energy and prefactor are mixture-specific and are not shown in the figure.

steps.title: How steep: the sensitivity
steps.note: The relative rate change per kelvin. It falls as T rises, so the rate is most sensitive at lower temperature.

steps.title: Local energy balance of the patch
steps.note: A lumped model: heat release (first term) against loss (second term). It is a teaching model, not the solver's equation.

steps.title: Linearising the exponent near T0
steps.note: Frank-Kamenetskii expansion. It turns the rate into e^theta, which is why a modest temperature rise has a large effect.

steps.title: Run away or not: the competition
steps.note: Semenov's condition in words: past a certain temperature, the release curve rises faster than the loss line, so the balance is unstable and the temperature runs away.

steps.title: Rate ratio for a temperature rise
steps.note: Used in the worked example below with an illustrative activation temperature, not a value from the figure.

steps.title: Burned-gas plateau from energy conservation
steps.note: Why the maximum stops rising: the heat available is bounded by the fuel. With temperature-dependent c_p and dissociation, the real plateau is lower than this crude estimate.

worked.title: How strongly does a hot spot respond to a temperature rise?
worked.problem: Take an illustrative activation temperature E_a/R = 20000 K (an assumed teaching value, not the value used in this simulation). By what factor does the rate change when the patch at 1250 K warms by 100 K?

solution.text: Linear estimate of the exponent for 100 K.

worked.answer: About 3.6 (a rate increase of 360 percent, from 1.3 percent per kelvin) for a rise of 100 K, using the local linearisation. The exact ratio with 1/T is slightly smaller, but the order of magnitude, a few times, is the point: the hotter the patch, the faster it heats itself.

analyze.q: If the patch were slightly colder or smaller, what would the red curve do, and what would the fourth snapshot look like?
analyze.hint: The release curve must not overtake the loss line.

analyze.q: The maximum temperature falls slightly after 15 ms while the fuel consumed keeps rising. List two physical reasons.
analyze.hint: Expansion, heat loss to the surrounding gas, dilution by diffusion.

analyze.q: The blocky edge of the fourth snapshot shows only a few cells across the front. What quantities in this figure would you expect to change on a finer mesh?
analyze.hint: Kernel radius, ignition time, fuel consumed.

evaluate.q: Is one run enough to say the hot spot ignites 'at 6.6 ms'? What would a defensible ignition time need?
evaluate.hint: A stated criterion, such as a temperature threshold or maximum rate, and mesh and time-step sensitivity.

evaluate.q: The figure shows temperature and consumed fuel but not composition or pressure. What does the reader need before comparing with a published ignition delay?

create: Redraw the bottom-left panel with a second y axis showing the heating rate dT/dt on a log scale, so the runaway is visible as a spike.
Design a set of nine runs (three patch temperatures by three patch sizes) and describe the single figure that would show the ignition boundary.

checks.q: Why does the domain-average temperature barely change at the moment of ignition?
checks.hint: How big is the burning region at that instant?
checks.answer: Because the ignited region is tiny compared with the whole domain. The average is dominated by the cold gas. The maximum shows the local event; the average only follows once the burning region has grown.

checks.q: With E_a/R = 20000 K at T = 1250 K, what is the relative rate change per kelvin?
checks.answer: 20000/1250^2 = 0.0128 per kelvin, about 1.3 percent per kelvin.

checks.q: The hottest-point curve shows a knee but the fuel curve shows none. Is this inconsistent?
checks.answer: No. Temperature in the hottest cell responds quickly to a high local rate, while consumed fuel integrates over the region and over time. A steep temperature knee and a smooth consumption curve are normal.

checks.q: What would convince you that the plateau temperature is physical?
checks.answer: A comparison with the adiabatic flame temperature of the same mixture and pressure from an equilibrium calculation, with the plateau a little below it if dissociation or heat loss acts.

checks.q: How would you map the ignition boundary of hot spots?
checks.hint: A grid of patch sizes and temperatures.
checks.answer: Run a grid of patch temperature and radius, record ignited or not by a fixed criterion (for example the maximum reaching a threshold within a time limit), and plot the outcomes on the plane with the boundary between the two outcomes drawn.
